rationale: I'm re-referencing each recording to the common average before computing the Welch PSD. Right now every channel's spectrum is mixed with the activity of whatever reference electrode the amplifier used (linked ears, Cz, and so on). That hides the topography of the known schizophrenia effects (more frontal delta/theta, less posterior alpha). It also makes the features depend on the reference, which is a problem for the external MSU and RepOD sets that use different hardware. I haven't run this, so I don't yet know whether it changes the Dev score.

I'm making the spectrum robust to reference and artifacts. Each recording is re-referenced to the common average, and Welch segments are averaged with the median instead of the mean, before computing relative band power. ASEEG and the external sets use different original references and have no artifact rejection, so a single eye-blink, muscle or electrode-pop segment can skew mean-averaged band power. The median-Welch, average-reference spectrum should track the delta/theta increase and alpha decrease seen in schizophrenia more reliably, and carry over better to MSU and RepOD.

I'm changing only the preprocessing. Each recording is re-referenced to the common average, and the Welch spectrum uses the median across segments instead of the mean. The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink or movement segments can dominate a mean spectrum. The median down-weights those segments, and the common average removes the original reference, so the relative band power should be more stable and transfer better to the external amplifiers. The classifier and features stay the same.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few large transients (blinks, movement, electrode pops) can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and blur the subject's band-power profile. This change only switches Welch to median averaging across the 2-s segments, which down-weights artifact segments. Every other part of the pipeline stays the same. It should also hold up better on the short, noisier external recordings.

I'm making one preprocessing change: re-reference each recording to the common average, then average the Welch segments by their median instead of their mean. The data has no artifact rejection and uses each clinic's original reference, so short blink/muscle bursts and reference differences distort the per-channel relative power. Median segments resist those bursts, and the average reference makes the topography less dependent on the external amplifiers (MSU/RepOD). That should give a cleaner, more transferable view of the known schizophrenia slowing (more delta/theta, less alpha).

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD can be pulled off by a few segments with blinks, movement or muscle bursts. That mostly inflates delta and gamma power and hides the slow-wave and alpha differences seen in schizophrenia. This change takes the median across the 2-s Welch segments instead of the mean, which makes the per-channel spectrum robust to those transient artifacts and to recording length. Nothing else changes.

I'm making one change to how the spectrum is estimated, in two parts. First, each recording is re-referenced to the common average, so the features no longer depend on the clinic's original reference; that matters when the model is applied to the MSU and RepOD sets. Second, Welch segments are combined with a median instead of a mean, so short high-amplitude artifacts (blinks, movement, electrode pops) in this unprocessed data have less pull on band power, while the relative-power features and the classifier stay the same.

I'm splitting alpha into 8–10 and 10–13 Hz and beta into 13–20 and 20–30 Hz. Schizophrenia often slows the alpha rhythm, which moves power from upper to lower alpha, and it also changes beta. The current 8–13 Hz band adds both alpha halves together and hides that shift. The extra relative-power features stay label-free and still carry over when amplitude scale or reference changes.

Welch's mean over 2-s segments lets a few artifact bursts (eye/head movement in delta, muscle in beta/gamma) dominate the spectrum. These 5-min recordings have had no artifact rejection, so I'm switching the per-segment aggregation to the median. This is a robust, label-free form of artifact handling that should give cleaner subject-level band powers, and it also holds up better on the short, noisier external recordings.

I'm re-referencing each recording to the common average and switching Welch from mean to median averaging across segments. The external sets (MSU, RepOD) use other amplifiers and references, and the recordings here have no artifact rejection. An average reference removes the effect of the original reference electrode, so the relative-band topography is comparable across sites. The median across 2-s segments stops a few blink, muscle or movement segments from dominating the spectrum, which should give a more stable delta/theta/alpha profile for schizophrenia.

These recordings have no artifact rejection, so short bursts of blinks, movement or muscle noise can inflate the mean Welch spectrum, especially in the delta and gamma bands, and can hide the slowing reported in schizophrenia. I'm switching Welch to a median over segments, which gives a spectrum robust to those bursts and to recording length (1 min on MSU, 5 min here). Features, scaling and classifier stay the same.

I'm changing only the preprocessing: re-reference each recording to the common average, then estimate the spectrum with a median-averaged Welch instead of a mean-averaged one. Recordings come with their original reference and no artifact rejection, so the relative band powers are skewed by reference-electrode activity and by brief high-amplitude artifacts like blinks and movement. Both fixes should give cleaner schizophrenia spectral markers (slow-wave excess, reduced alpha) that also hold up on the external MSU and RepOD sets, which use different amplifiers and references.

Schizophrenia is associated with slower alpha peak frequency and changes in the aperiodic (1/f) part of the spectrum, which relative band power only partly captures. This change adds two features per channel: the aperiodic exponent, fitted on log-log 2–40 Hz with the alpha range left out, and the peak alpha frequency, taken as the centre of gravity of 7–13 Hz power after removing the 1/f fit. Neither depends on amplitude scale, so both should also hold up on the external datasets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few large blinks, movements or electrode pops can dominate the default mean-averaged Welch PSD and distort relative band power (especially delta and gamma). Taking the median across Welch segments (`average="median"`) is a robust spectral estimate that ignores these transient artifacts. It should help more on the short, noisy external recordings, and nothing else in the pipeline changes. This hasn't been run yet, so I don't have a new score.

Slower individual alpha peak frequency is one of the most reproducible resting-state EEG findings in schizophrenia, and relative band power with fixed 8–13 Hz edges cannot capture it. This change adds a per-channel alpha centre-of-gravity frequency (7–13 Hz, from a 4 s median-averaged Welch PSD to resist artifacts) plus its median across channels. Both are frequency-based, so they are unaffected by amplitude scale and recording length on the external sets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few eye-movement, muscle or electrode-pop segments can dominate the mean-averaged Welch spectrum. Averaging the 2-s segments by median instead (`average="median"`) is a robust spectral estimate. It should give band powers that better reflect the subject's ongoing background EEG, where schizophrenia shows extra slow-wave and less alpha activity. It should also travel better to the external clinics, whose recordings and noise levels differ.

Slowing of the individual alpha peak is one of the most consistently replicated resting EEG findings in schizophrenia. I'm adding a per-channel alpha center-of-gravity frequency (7–13 Hz, from a 4 s median-Welch PSD) next to the existing log relative band powers. The feature is measured in Hz, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on the external sets. I haven't run it, so I don't have a Dev score for this version yet.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few blinks, movement bursts or muscle-contaminated segments can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD and shift relative band power. My hypothesis is that taking the median across Welch segments instead (`average="median"`) will give a more artifact-robust spectrum per subject. That should make the SZ-related spectral shifts (more slow-wave power, less alpha) stand out more clearly, and help more on short, noisy external recordings. The features and classifier are otherwise unchanged.

I'm changing the reference to the common average before computing the Welch PSD. The recordings keep their original reference, and the external clinics (MSU, RepOD) use different montages, so a reference-free montage should make the relative band powers describe local cortical activity (for example the frontal/temporal delta-theta rise and posterior alpha drop reported in schizophrenia). It also makes the model more consistent across sites. I haven't run this, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

I'm adding a per-channel alpha peak frequency feature (centre of gravity of the 7–13 Hz spectrum, plus a whole-head average) to the log relative band powers. Slower alpha peak frequency is a well-replicated eyes-closed EEG finding in schizophrenia. The feature is a frequency, not an amplitude, so it is not affected by amplifier scale or reference choice, and a 4 s Welch window gives the finer frequency resolution it needs.
